c.tagline: Antebellum charm of cobblestone streets, Rainbow Row, and Lowcountry cooking.

taxi.fareNote: Street taxis are metered but scarce on the peninsula; app-based Uber and Lyft are the norm and usually cheaper, with pedicabs and horse carriages for short historic-district hops.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 311 is the city's non-emergency line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The historic peninsula has no no-go zones, though parts of the upper peninsula and some North Charleston neighborhoods have higher crime and little visitor interest.
Late-night King Street bar crowds bring occasional petty theft and rowdiness; park in lit garages rather than isolated streets.

hood_desc: Charleston's most prestigious historic quarter at the tip of the peninsula, lined with grand antebellum mansions, the Battery seawall promenade, White Point Garden, and the pastel townhouses of Rainbow Row; best for first-timers who want the postcard Charleston within walking distance.

A compact, gallery-filled historic district around the Dock Street Theatre, cobblestone Chalmers Street, and historic churches; suits travelers who want art, architecture, and fine dining steps from the waterfront.

The peninsula's main spine of shopping, restaurants, and rooftop bars — antiques at the lower end, boutiques mid-street, and buzzing nightlife on Upper King; best for those who want to eat, drink, and shop in the heart of downtown.

A relaxed, family-friendly suburb across the Cooper River bridge with Shem Creek's seafood docks, Sullivan's Island and Isle of Palms beaches nearby, and Patriots Point; good for a quieter, car-based base near the water.
A laid-back barrier-island beach town southeast of the city — surf breaks, a fishing pier, casual seafood shacks and a bohemian vibe; suits travelers who want sand and sea over historic sightseeing.
lodging: The Beach Club at Charleston Harbor Resort
Extended Stay America Suites - Charleston - Mt Pleasant

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.pay: CARTA buses take exact cash ($2 a ride) or the Token Transit mobile app; the DASH trolley loops through the historic downtown and is free. A CARTA day pass is about $7.
transit.hours: CARTA buses run roughly 5am to midnight on core routes; the free DASH trolley runs daytime into the evening, with late-night trips filled by ride-hailing.
transit.note: Charleston has no rail or metro transit; the CARTA bus network plus the free DASH trolley through the historic district are the public options, and the compact peninsula is very walkable.

transit.m: CARTA bus to North Charleston, connect toward downtown (~45 min)
Ride-hail or taxi to the historic district (20-30 min)

tip.r: ~18-20% at restaurants; $1-2 per drink at bars and ~15% for taxi or ride-hail.

landmarks: Rainbow Row
Thirteen candy-colored Georgian townhouses along East Bay Street form America's most photographed pastel streetscape, a symbol of Charleston's antebellum charm.
The Battery and White Point Garden
Oak-shaded promenade where stately mansions face the harbor, Civil War cannons dot the lawns, and Fort Sumter shimmers across the water.
Fort Sumter National Monument
The harbor island fort where Confederate guns opened the Civil War in April 1861, reached by scenic boat tour past dolphins and pelicans.
Waterfront Park and the Pineapple Fountain
A graceful harborside park whose splashing pineapple-shaped fountain, symbol of Southern hospitality, and swinging bench piers invite long, breezy lingering.
Charleston City Market
Four blocks of open-air halls dating to 1804, where Gullah artisans weave famed sweetgrass baskets amid stalls of local food and crafts.
St. Michael's Church
Charleston's oldest church building, a 1761 white-steepled beauty at the Four Corners of Law, where George Washington and Robert E. Lee both worshipped.
Magnolia Plantation and Gardens
America's oldest public gardens drape Spanish moss and azaleas over romantic black-water swamps at this 1676 Ashley River plantation.
Angel Oak
A cathedral-like live oak on Johns Island, estimated 400-500 years old, whose sprawling limbs shade 17,000 square feet of hushed, sacred-feeling ground.
Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge
The elegant twin-diamond cable-stayed bridge soaring over the Cooper River invites walkers and cyclists to earn skyline-and-harbor views from its dedicated lane.
Nathaniel Russell House
An 1808 neoclassical merchant's mansion celebrated for its gravity-defying free-flying spiral staircase and meticulously restored Federal-period interiors.

train.note: Two Amtrak trains call daily: the Palmetto, a daytime train between New York and Savannah, and the Silver Meteor, an overnight New York to Miami service with sleeping cars. Both use the North Charleston Intermodal Transportation Center at 4565 Gaynor Avenue, roughly ten miles and 20-30 minutes from the historic downtown peninsula, so budget for a taxi or rideshare - there is no quick transit link. The Silver Meteor's Charleston stops fall in the middle of the night in both directions. There are no international trains in the American Southeast.

bus.note: There are no international coach routes from Charleston; the nearest border is thousands of miles away. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) and FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) handle the long-distance runs, typically around two hours to Savannah, two to Columbia, four to Charlotte and five to Atlanta, with tickets bought online. Local CARTA buses (https://www.ridecarta.com/) connect the North Charleston transport centre and the airport with downtown, and CARTA's free DASH shuttles circulate the historic district.

intl.to: Fort Sumter National Monument (USA) - departs Liberty Square, 340 Concord Street downtown, and Patriots Point in Mount Pleasant

ferry.note: The Fort Sumter boat is the only way to reach the island where the Civil War began - private vessels may not dock there - and the harbour crossing takes about 30 minutes each way, with a similar time ashore. Sailings run year round but are far more frequent from spring to autumn and sell out in summer, so book online ahead. The Charleston Water Taxi also shuttles across the harbour between downtown and Patriots Point in Mount Pleasant. No long-distance or international ferries call at Charleston; the port handles containers and cruise ships.
